notes.meaning: Saul gives up on secret schemes and openly commands his son Jonathan and all his attendants to kill David. Jonathan loves David dearly, creating a clash between loyalty to his father the king and love for an innocent friend. God uses Jonathan's devotion to protect David from sudden destruction.

Jonathan immediately warns David of the danger and tells him to hide in a secret spot in the field until morning. He plans to stand near his father in the open country so he can sound him out about David and report back right away. Jonathan risks his father's anger to keep his covenant of friendship.

Jonathan speaks up bravely for David, reminding Saul that David has never harmed him and has brought only great benefits to the kingdom. He recalls how David risked his life to strike down Goliath, bringing victory to Israel while Saul looked on with joy. Jonathan urges his father not to bring the guilt of shedding innocent blood upon his royal house.

Saul listens to Jonathan's plea and takes an oath in the name of the Lord that David will not be put to death. Jonathan shares the good news with David and brings him back into Saul's presence, restoring him to his former duties at court. For a brief season, wise words restore peace to the palace.

War flares up again with the Philistines, and David marches out to battle. He wins a crushing victory over Israel's enemies and forces them to flee. Instead of holding back out of fear, David faithfully serves his country once more.

David's latest battlefield honors revive Saul's jealousy, and a distressing spirit permitted by the Lord comes over the king. As David plays his harp to soothe him, Saul hurls his spear with such force that it sticks into the wall. David dodges the blow just in time and slips away into the night.

Saul sends armed guards to surround David's home and wait until dawn to kill him when he walks outside. David's wife Michal discovers the plot and warns him that he will be dead by morning if he does not escape at once. She helps him climb down through a back window, and he flees to safety under cover of darkness.

Michal takes a life-sized household idol and arranges it in the bed under a blanket to buy David time. She places a piece of goat hair near the top to look like David's hair in the dim bedroom light. When Saul's guards arrive to seize David, she tells them that he is too sick to leave his bed.

Saul is so thirsty for David's blood that he orders the messengers to carry the bed itself to him so he can kill David with his own hands. When the men enter the room to lift the bed, they discover only the carved wooden idol and the goat hair. Saul's cruel scheme is completely exposed and frustrated.

Saul angrily demands to know why Michal betrayed him by helping his enemy get away. Michal protects herself by claiming that David threatened to kill her if she did not help him escape. While her quick thinking saved David's life, she shielded herself with a lie that tarnished her husband's good name.

David travels directly to Samuel at Ramah and tells the elderly prophet everything Saul has done to him. Samuel takes David to Naioth, a settlement where the company of prophets lived and studied God's word. David wisely seeks godly guidance and worship when his earthly life is thrown into chaos.

Saul sends three separate groups of officers to Naioth to capture David. Each group finds Samuel leading the prophets in holy songs of praise, and the Spirit of God overpowers the soldiers so that they drop their mission and begin praising God as well. God easily turns would-be captors into worshippers to defend His servant.

Saul decides to travel to Ramah himself, stopping at the large cistern at Secu to confirm where Samuel and David are staying. As he walks toward Naioth, the Spirit of God comes upon Saul as well, causing him to walk along chanting praises before he even reaches the town. God meets the angry king on the road and stops his violent purpose in its tracks.

Saul strips off his royal robes and armor, prophesying before Samuel until he collapses on the ground for a full day and night. This dramatic scene revives the old saying, 'Is Saul also among the prophets?' God humbles the proud king and leaves him helpless on the floor so that David has plenty of time to escape safely.
